name: Congenital radioulnar synostosis
aliases: congenital fusion of the forearm bones

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A bony or fibrous bridge unites the proximal radius and ulna, so forearm rotation (pronation and supination) is absent or severely restricted while the elbow and wrist may move normally
The forearm is characteristically fixed in pronation, and the degree of fixed pronation determines the functional disability
Presentation is often delayed because children compensate with shoulder and wrist motion; difficulty with supination-dependent tasks (accepting coins, catching, self-feeding) prompts recognition
It is frequently bilateral and may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities (including sex-chromosome aneuploidies) and other syndromes
Radiographs confirm the proximal fusion; the radial head may be absent, hypoplastic, or dislocated posteriorly
Mild deformity with acceptable pronation frequently needs no treatment, and surgery is considered only for severe fixed pronation limiting function
Surgery is usually a derotational osteotomy to reposition the forearm nearer neutral rather than an attempt to restore rotation, because recreating a mobile joint is unreliable and prone to re-fusion
reference.pathophysiology: Early in limb development the proximal radius and ulna share a common cartilaginous anlage and normally undergo longitudinal segmentation to separate; congenital radioulnar synostosis reflects a failure of this differentiation, leaving the bones fused proximally. Because the forearm forms in a pronated position, the fused segment locks the limb in fixed pronation. The abnormality is therefore one of failure of differentiation and segmentation rather than of formation, and it may be linked to genetic or chromosomal disturbances, which explains its frequent bilaterality and syndromic associations.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital dislocation of the radial head without synostosis
Pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow), which is transient
Arthrogryposis affecting the elbow and forearm
Multiple hereditary exostoses tethering the forearm
Malunion after a forearm fracture limiting rotation
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the forearm and elbow to confirm proximal fusion and assess the radial head
CT with three-dimensional reconstruction to define the bony bridge before surgical planning
Clinical measurement of the forearm rotation arc and the fixed pronation angle
Karyotype or targeted genetic evaluation when syndromic features or bilateral involvement are present
Examination for associated musculoskeletal anomalies in other limbs, the hips, and the knees
redFlags: Severe fixed hyperpronation of both forearms causing major functional limitation
An associated syndromic or chromosomal disorder requiring broader assessment
Neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome following a large corrective osteotomy
reference.prognosis: Many children function surprisingly well through compensatory shoulder and wrist motion and need no intervention; when correction is required, derotational osteotomy reliably improves the resting position of the hand, although forearm rotation itself is not restored and large corrections carry a risk of neurovascular complications.
pitfalls: Attempting to excise the synostosis to restore rotation, which commonly re-fuses and disappoints
Over-correcting the derotational osteotomy and precipitating compartment syndrome or neurovascular injury
Missing bilaterality and an associated syndrome
Delaying diagnosis because unilateral cases compensate so well
management: Manage mild deformity with acceptable resting pronation by observation alone, since compensatory shoulder and wrist motion usually preserves function
Reserve derotational osteotomy of the fused segment for severe fixed pronation that limits function, repositioning the hand into a more neutral posture (forearm rotation itself is not restored)
Provide occupational therapy and adaptive strategies for supination-dependent tasks such as self-feeding and receiving objects
Monitor for neurovascular compromise after large corrections, staging or limiting the correction to reduce this risk
Arrange karyotype or targeted genetic evaluation when the synostosis is bilateral or syndromic, and screen for associated anomalies of the other limbs, hips and knees
Offer genetic counselling to families given the association with chromosomal and syndromic disorders
